clue.text: Poseur disposed to accept large bill? How absurd

indicators.note: to accept tells us the rearranged poseur takes another piece into its middle
disposed in the sense of arranged or set out anew, so the letters of poseur are reordered

parts.note: a poster is a large bill stuck up on a wall

explanation.surface: A show-off is happy to take on a huge bill, which is ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposed' rearranges POSEUR to PRE...OUS, and 'to accept' sets POSTER inside it. 'bill' wants to be money owed; here it is a printed notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Something outrageous to the point of being laughable is preposterous, the exclamation saying how ridiculous it is.

clue.text: Mole takes in ace path-finder

indicators.note: takes in says the first word swallows the next piece inside it

parts.note: a mole is a harbour breakwater or jetty, a pier
an ace counts as one in cards and dice

explanation.surface: A burrowing animal swallows a playing card and then leads the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mole' looks like the animal or a spy; here it is a stone jetty, PIER, which 'takes in' ONE after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pioneer is the first to explore and open up a route, a trailblazer.

clue.text: The day of the goose?

parts.note: one word goes before both day and goose: the church's quarterly fast days, and an old name for the great northern diver

explanation.walkthrough: Ember days are four sets of fasting days in the church year; the ember-goose is an old name for the great northern diver, a seabird.
explanation.definitionFit: The word qualifies both the church fast days and an old bird name, so it is the word 'of' both.

clue.text: Constrained (but not stumped) to change decree

indicators.note: to change says the remaining letters are to be rearranged
but not tells us a piece is to be left out of the word before it

parts.note: st is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped

explanation.surface: Someone forced, though not baffled, to alter an official order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not' removes ST, cricket's abbreviation for stumped, from CONSTRAINED, leaving CONRAINED, which 'to change' rearranges. 'stumped' looks like 'baffled'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an authoritative order or regulation, such as a by-law.

clue.text: Occasion for the landlord to call

definitions.meaning: an occasion is a particular moment or instance
a British pub landlord shouts this word at closing to end drinking

explanation.surface: A pub owner decides when it is the right moment to ring.
explanation.walkthrough: British pubs close with the landlord calling this word ('last orders, please!'), a cultural custom.
explanation.definitionFit: An occasion is a point or instance, as in 'this time'; and it is the publican's closing cry.

clue.text: Railmen raised a barrier for the old fugitive

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the piece is written from bottom to top

parts.note: the NUR was the National Union of Railwaymen, a British trade union
a gate is a barrier across an opening

explanation.surface: Railway workers put up a gate to stop an escaped prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns NUR (the National Union of Railwaymen, a British union) upside down in a down entry to give RUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Runagate is an archaic word for a runaway or vagabond, hence 'old'.

clue.text: Complaint of the 13 fraternity

definitions.meaning: a minor ailment, as a stomach disorder
13 is the answer to the clue for 13-across, so the clue means a word from the horse-riding world: a rider thrown off

explanation.surface: A grievance raised by members of a numbered brotherhood.
explanation.walkthrough: '13' points to the 13-across answer, the world of riding; a rider who is thrown has suffered an upset.
explanation.definitionFit: A stomach ailment is called an upset; and for horsemen, being tipped out of the saddle is a spill of the same name.

clue.text: Shrink from such an undertaking

definitions.meaning: to shrink is to become smaller

explanation.surface: Someone recoils from taking on so large a task.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, to shy away from a task; split it into a verb and a noun phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Muscles shrink when they tighten up; and a formal agreement is a legally binding deal.

clue.text: Fine for being caught in a lake

indicators.note: in says the abbreviation sits inside the word for the lake

parts.note: a mere is a lake or pond
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A penalty imposed on someone found fishing illegally in a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like a noun, a penalty; here it is the verb, to impose a fine. C (cricket's caught) goes into MERE.
explanation.definitionFit: To amerce is an old legal verb for punishing by an arbitrary monetary penalty.

clue.text: Complaints investigator gives order to Flanagan's valet

parts.note: OM stands for the Order of Merit, a British honour
Bud Flanagan was a British music-hall comedian, so his manservant is Bud's man

explanation.surface: An official probing grievances gives instructions to a comedian's manservant.
explanation.walkthrough: Bud Flanagan was a British comedian of the Crazy Gang; his man is BUD'S MAN. OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: An ombudsman is an official appointed to look into grievances against organisations.

clue.text: Unjustified excitement at the tea-table?

parts.note: a fuss over nothing is said to happen in a teacup, the idiom that the clue pictures

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is 'a storm in a teacup' (US 'tempest in a teapot'), a great fuss about something trivial.
explanation.definitionFit: An uproar or outburst is a storm; the teacup idiom makes it an overblown one.

clue.text: Some traveller ran there seeking adventure

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A wanderer went off to find excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight-errant roams in search of adventure, so errant means wandering on a quest.

clue.text: Kitchen revolutionary?

parts.note: the revolutionary here is not political but a part that turns round and round inside a washing machine

explanation.walkthrough: An agitator is the paddle in a washing machine that churns the clothes, so it revolves in the kitchen; it is also a political rabble-rouser.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrer of political unrest is an agitator, and so is the rotating paddle of a washer.

clue.text: Bicycling in Yorkshire once

definitions.meaning: Yorkshire was formerly divided into three administrative areas called by this name

explanation.surface: Cycling round the north of England in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire, a large English county, was historically divided into North, East and West Ridings.
explanation.definitionFit: Being astride and travelling on a bike is riding; and the old divisions of Yorkshire were thirds bearing that name.

clue.text: Cynic? Gide's one, maybe

indicators.note: maybe says the letters that follow are only one possible arrangement

parts.note: the possessive is taken as written, its s included

explanation.surface: A doubter asks whether a character belongs to the French novelist Gide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges GIDE'S ONE. Andre Gide was a French novelist; the Greek philosopher in the answer was the most famous of the Cynic school.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek philosopher who lived in a tub founded the Cynic school, so he is the archetypal Cynic.

clue.text: Cessation of work means reduction in pay

definitions.meaning: a halt to work, as in a strike

explanation.surface: A strike means workers lose wages.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage, stoppages are deductions from wages for tax or insurance.
explanation.definitionFit: A strike is a halt in production; and deductions withheld from wages are called by the same word.

clue.text: Anybody in France with fifty employees

parts.note: personne is French for anybody (or nobody)
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Anyone in France who has fifty workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Personnel are the staff of an organisation.

clue.text: She's entitled to obstruct a particular vessel

parts.note: to bar is to obstruct
one, as in 'one day', means a particular
SS stands for steamship, a vessel

explanation.surface: A woman claims the right to block a certain ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entitled' looks like 'has the right'; here it means holding a title.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman holding a noble title, such as a life peer, is a baroness.

clue.text: Bishop once said to be turbulent

indicators.note: turbulent means stirred up, so the letters of once said are churned

explanation.surface: A churchman was formerly said to be troublesome, recalling Henry II's turbulent priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be turbulent' rearranges ONCE SAID. The surface echoes Henry II's 'turbulent priest', Thomas Becket.
explanation.definitionFit: A diocesan is the bishop in charge of a diocese, as opposed to an assistant bishop.

clue.text: Oppressor from Continental location

parts.note: de is French for from
a spot is a place or location

explanation.surface: A tyrant hails from a place in mainland Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from Continental' reads as where the oppressor comes from; it is the French word for 'from'.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is a tyrant ruling with absolute power.

clue.text: It's very cold for Noah's bloodsucker, I hear

indicators.note: I hear says the words are spoken and the answer sounds like them

parts.note: Noah's boat was the ark, and a tick is a bloodsucking parasite

explanation.surface: A parasite on Noah's boat finds the weather freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: An ARK TICK, a tick aboard Noah's ark, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Polar conditions are bitterly cold, so arctic is used for anything freezing.

clue.text: Many an ambiguous utterance produced by craft

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a conventional many
the Delphic oracle gave famously ambiguous pronouncements

explanation.surface: Plenty of double-edged remarks come from cunning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' looks like cunning; it is a boat. C (100) is a crossword 'many'.
explanation.definitionFit: A coracle is a small round boat of wicker and hide, a craft.

clue.text: A source of humiliation, though not for Mother Hubbard?

definitions.text: A source of humiliation, though not for Mother Hubbard?

parts.words: A source of humiliation, though not for Mother Hubbard?
parts.note: an embarrassing secret is hidden in the cupboard, but in the nursery rhyme Old Mother Hubbard's cupboard was bare

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is 'a skeleton in the cupboard', a shameful secret; in the nursery rhyme Old Mother Hubbard's cupboard held nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden scandal is a skeleton in the cupboard.

clue.text: Appear on stage and make a record

definitions.meaning: come on to the stage in a play
write in a ledger or register

explanation.surface: An actor comes on and cuts a disc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make a record' looks like recording music; it means to write an item into a list.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage directions say a character comes on with this word; and to log data in a book is to put it down there.

clue.text: Bandsman responsible for the takings?

parts.note: the band is not musical but a gang, and its takings are stolen goods rather than box-office money

explanation.walkthrough: A bandsman suggests a musician, and takings suggest the till; the band is a gang of thieves, and takings are loot.
explanation.definitionFit: A thief who belongs to a gang and seizes property is a robber.

clue.text: Fish-headed god from this island?

parts.note: bar is an old name for the maigre, a large sea fish
Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: An Egyptian deity with a fish's head comes from this island.
explanation.walkthrough: Ra the sun god is 'headed' by a fish, BAR. Barra is an island in Scotland's Outer Hebrides.
explanation.definitionFit: Barra is one of the Outer Hebrides off the west coast of Scotland.

clue.text: Cliff's second vehicle

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Cliff owns a second car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cliff's' reads as the singer Cliff Richard's; it is the noun followed by 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a steep rocky crag or cliff face, especially in northern England.

clue.text: It's patent that a harmonic lacks one

indicators.note: lacks says the harmonic is missing a piece

parts.note: an overtone is a harmonic above the fundamental note

explanation.surface: It is clear that a musical tone is missing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'patent' looks like an invention licence; here it means plain to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Patent in the sense of plain and open matches overt, done openly.

clue.text: Odd way to go from one movement to another

definitions.text: way to go from one movement to another
definitions.meaning: in machinery a disc mounted off-centre on a shaft turns rotation into back-and-forth motion

explanation.surface: A strange route from one artistic movement to the next.
explanation.walkthrough: In engineering, an off-centre wheel converts rotary motion into reciprocating motion.
explanation.definitionFit: A strange person is said to be off-centre; and the off-centre mechanical cam bears that name too.

clue.text: Means of informing crowd about duration of tenure

parts.note: to press is a throng or crowd
re means about or concerning
a lease is the period for which property is held

explanation.surface: A way of telling the crowd how long a tenancy lasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'informing crowd' reads as one phrase; split it after 'informing'.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement issued to the newspapers to announce something is a press release.
